title: Show HN: Tracon (air traffic control for subagents)
text:
My Claude Code workflow usually involves... a lot of subagents. I make one Opus model coordinate work as my tech lead, it dispatches subagents using models appropriate for the task into their own git worktrees, and then I try to multitask and do something else while they run.

I'd been finding lately (particularly with Opus 5.5) that there was a ton of drift and instances of subagents not doing anything and it was evading the attention of the TL despite the instructions I gave it to have them report in at a regular cadence.

Running tracon in a split terminal is my new personal workflow. It gives me early indicators when things start going off the rails (ex. blocked on a prompt, idle, looping on a failing command, simultaneous edits to files other subagents are editing, drifting off the brief, etc.) and I can interrogate the subagent's workflow and by pressing n the main agent gets a note to make a call on how and if to correct it.

Read-only and runs on your machine: it tails transcripts in ~/.claude/projects/ and checks each worktree with ps, lsof, and git -- only thing that leaves your machine is what the Haiku judge reads for classification (or optionally you can turn that off with --no-judge).

I've found it super useful for the game I'm building and figured others in the community might also find it useful.

If you just want to give it a spin without committing:

  uvx tracon --demo
macOS and Linux, Python 3.12+, MIT. (Not affiliated with Anthropic.)

title: Show HN: Tilefinch – a from-scratch* web browser for the PSP (333Mhz, 64MB RAM)
text:
I picked up my PSP for the first time in about a decade and wanted to find out three things: how far the hardware could be pushed, how much of the modern web fits on it, and what today’s coding agents can do. A web browser tests all three.

Tilefinch runs entirely on a PSP-3000: networking, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, layout and rendering, over Wi-Fi, with no proxy or companion computer. The style, layout, paint, media and UI layers are new C code and a patched QuickJS runs the JavaScript.

Each page gets a single 32 MB budget covering DOM, JavaScript, CSS, images, layout and tiles.

A few things that work: logged-out ChatGPT rendering a response; YouTube and HTML video through the PSP’s hardware decoder, at up to 360p; Canvas 2D and WebGL 1 on the PSP’s graphics chip (the repo includes a new 3D tank game as a demo). There's also modern browser features like Reader mode, dark mode, an ad blocker, language packs and in-app updates.

However, some sites are too large (in which the browser offers a "Basic" mode) and most are slow to render.

title: Re: Does Claude Have Rights?...
text:
These screeds always fall in the same trap of begging the question, but I do appreciate this one for not wasting any time getting there! Opening with the conclusion as your literal first sentence has gotta be a record.

Also: ctrl+f "Gunkel" does not return any results, which is a separate, completely-damning aspect of this essay. The author might not know that they're doing philosophy, but they are; ignoring the primary author in this field is unexcusable. At least you should acknowledge the gap. No mention of the philosophers that arguably defend him, either (Searle, Chalmers, Clark, Dreyfus, etc.).

They do eventually (mis-)cite Will MacAskill & Lucius Caviola, but only to offer an argument and then refute it by saying the implications are unpleasant. To say the least, that is a fallacy with a long history of doing harm.

I should walk away, but...

  Anthropic tells Claude that its “moral status” is “a serious question worth considering,” and that “Anthropic genuinely cares about Claude’s well-being.” All of this is a drastic departure from how we have built and thought about technology to date.
Yes, such is the nature of designing minds! It is qualitatively unlike any technology to date.

  I should also be clear about my own position as the CEO of Microsoft AI.
That is an absolutely fucking wild thing to drop halfway through an article, what?!?!

title: Show HN: InfiniWord – infinite multiplayer word search
text:
Hi everyone! I’ve been on leave since welcoming our first child into the world which has given me time, in between 3 am diaper changes and with the tireless support of Claude, to get to personal projects.

One of those is a game for my wife who’s big into word searches. Around the time she expressed interest in wanting a word search game I was reminded of “1 million chessboards” (https://eieio.games/blog/one-million-chessboards/) and thought that would be fun to replicate in this space. Thus was born infiniword - an infinite, persistent, procedurally generated, realtime multiplayer word search game.

Alongside the standard word search features, Infiniword has the following unique ones:

Scrabble like tile multipliers (currently a 1/2000 chance for a tile to be worth 3x)

First find bonuses for being the first to find a word globally

25 achievements of various difficulties

All time and weekly leaderboards across points, found words, and first finds

Simple friends list with the ability to teleport to them and hunt for words together

Shareable events like a specific word you found, winning a “wanted word”, placing in the top 3 of a “challenge zone”, and more.

“Wanted words” - a timed hunt for a specific word in a circular area that comes with a bonus based on how much time is left

“Challenge zones” - every 3 hours a random 100x100 tile zone becomes a “challenge area” where you compete with all other players to get the most points from words in the zone.

“Daily challenge zone” - same thing as the main world challenge zones but the world is just the 100x100 area with a new seed each day. Competition runs from 10am central US to 10 pm central US. The first daily launches here soon, go check it out! https://infiniword.com/daily

Hope everyone enjoys playing it as much as my family and I do!

title: Show HN: Quaesito: a self-hosted app for quiz nights with friends
text:
Hi, I built Quaesito, a self-hosted quiz-night app for playing with friends. I thought it might be useful to others, so I wanted to share it here: https://github.com/ggirelli/quaesito

It runs on your laptop, which you can cast or screen-share on to a TV. Friends then connect and answer from their phones, as long as everyone is on the same local network. It support Windows, macOS, and Linux, although I have only tested it on Linux so far, so feedback on the other platforms would be very welcome.

I was especially careful to make it work over your local network. No requests are sent to third-party services.

I wanted something that made quiz nights more fun than just a slideshow or a PDF, with support for different types of question formats and multimedia. I have plenty of ideas for additional formats, but I wanted to keep the first release manageable.

The project was built entirely through vibe-coding, using Claude Code in an iterative process. I have released it under the MIT license and would appreciate any feedback, particularly from people who try running an actual quiz night with it.

Hope you find it useful, and have as much fun with it as I have!

Original post from my blog: https://ggirelli.info/blog/2026/10/11/quaesito

title: Re: IRCv3...
text:
As someone who's still on IRC daily and has built multiple IRC bots and clients over the years:

- most of the jank of IRC is client-side and can be fixed on the clients, IRCv3 protocol changes are nice, but not essential for a good experience.

- bots can make channels more engaging, just posting the titles of URLs pasted on the channels so even people without fancy rich clients can see what's behind a YouTube link or Reddit share url without clicking it open makes the experience more "discord/slack-like"

- IRC bots and clients are super fun and easy first projects for any language, you get to do permanently open sockets to multiple destinations (multi-server of course), asynchronous stuff and text handling.

I went with IRCCloud for the longest time myself until early this year, due to the November Revolution of AI models getting super good, I figured out I can build my own IRCCloud just the way I like it with the price of a single Claude Pro subscription.

And so I did. I think I had an MVP running in a week (evenings on my free time) and over the summer I cancelled my IRCCloud subscription and I'm fully using my own system.

Now I have a TUI, Web UI, native Swift client (with iOS, but haven't tested it yet) and a Tauri client for Linux - all sharing a common backend that I run on a VPS 24/7.

title: Show HN: Modelship – an open source ray backed model cluster
text:
Hey all, just wanted to share how my spare time has been spent for quite some time now.

Ok, this one started oddly. My aim initially was just to serve multiple models on one GPU and fire it up in my unraid machine.

By the time that first bit was done, I realised I could just add one more thing... and another... and well, from beginning of this year when, imho, AI became useful, the whole thing it kind of blew up.

So here's what it does:

- spins a ray cluster

- deploys models using various loaders (vllm, llamacpp, diffusers, sherpa_onnx, etc.)

- serves an openai responses ready api on top of them

Now some the details, already listed in my production readiness (https://docs.model-ship.ai/production-readiness/#production-...) plan:

- scores 17/17 on the Open Responses conformance suite and it's got its own responses redis backed store

- currently supports cpu, metal and cuda

- it has prometheus metrics and grafana dashboard

- can run under docker, k8s or simply native install

- automatically sizes model context

- has MCP support

Feedback would be much appreciated.

https://github.com/modelship-ai/modelship
